tldr: TornadoVM's library tasks let Java code mix its own GPU kernels with NVIDIA's cuFFT, cuBLAS, cuDNN and cuDF in one task graph, without JNI, Python or C++.
summary: The TornadoVM team starts from a familiar problem. Java runs the enterprise, but NVIDIA's tuned libraries (cuBLAS, cuFFT, cuDNN, CUTLASS, cuDF, cuVS) are reached through a Python sidecar, JNI or FFM bindings, or a C++ rewrite. TornadoVM works on any JDK 21+ distribution, compiles Java to OpenCL, CUDA PTX or Metal, and now offers four programming levels: the @Parallel loop annotation, the low-level KernelContext API, a new TileContext API that mirrors NVIDIA's tile programming model, and library tasks. A library task names a provider and calls a function such as cuFFT's R2C forward transform, with the same name and arguments as in the NVIDIA documentation, on FFM-backed data. It then chains in a task graph with Java-written JIT kernels, so data can stay on the GPU between steps.

Demos showed a low-pass filter built from cuFFT plus custom Java kernels, and a 'tile ladder' profiled with NVIDIA Nsight Systems. In that comparison the hand-tuned KernelContext and TileContext matrix multiplications reached about 90% of cuBLAS. The team's Java LLM inference engine on TornadoVM reached 90-95% of llama.cpp throughput on Gemma and Qwen models, and 12% better prefill in some cases, after being about 30x slower a year earlier. Mary Xekalaki showed Apache Flink SQL queries offloaded through a config flag to a task graph of cuDF Parquet reading, cuDF string matching and a JIT kernel, up to 17x faster on 64 million rows than one Flink slot (5x versus four slots). They also reported 90x faster JVector graph builds with Cassandra and 98% of hand-written CUDA kernel performance.
keyPoints: TornadoVM ships as JARs on Maven Central and SDKs via SDKMAN, and runs on OpenJDK, GraalVM, Temurin, Zulu and other JDK 21+ builds.
Library tasks are named so the runtime can optimise data movement across a task graph. Runtime features such as CUDA graphs, multiple streams and grid scheduling cut transfer overhead.
TileContext moves thread, prefetch and cache decisions to NVIDIA's compiler and is much more compact than equivalent KernelContext code using tensor-core MMA fragments.
Profiling combines JFR for the JVM side with NVIDIA Nsight for the GPU timeline, plus TornadoVM's own tools.
The Flink integration analyses the query IR and maps operations to library tasks where possible and JIT tasks otherwise, with no change to the SQL.
takeaways: Install TornadoVM via SDKMAN and run a first kernel on your laptop GPU before targeting NVIDIA servers.
Use library tasks for operations NVIDIA already optimises (GEMM, FFT, Parquet decode), and write only the glue steps as Java kernels.
Profile with JFR together with Nsight Systems to see where data transfers, not compute, dominate.

quotes.text: We have reached a point that Java can access the GPU like any other native.

watchIf: You want GPU acceleration or NVIDIA libraries in a Java application without JNI, Python or C++, and want to see actual performance numbers.
